entry.title: Every prompt has a footprint — so what?
entry.summary: A watt-hour means nothing to most people.
entry.content:
A watt-hour means nothing to most people. The same answer counted in phone charges or cups of coffee does. At the Digital Society School I helped build decision tools for the Dutch Ministry of Finance around exactly that translation — because the gap between the most and least efficient model on the same task can exceed an order of magnitude, and few tools put that in front of the person typing the prompt.

The point is not AI guilt. It's the same soft-path thinking I learned in water management: before you build a bigger pipe — or call a bigger model — ask whether the demand itself can be smarter. Try the EcoPrompt Coach chart on the homepage; that's the argument, running live.

Corrected October 2026: I left the Digital Society School in February 2026.

entry.title: Why I wrote a pessimistic future on purpose
entry.summary: Model output rarely moves a policymaker; a story they can picture does.
entry.content:
My Wageningen thesis ended with "Dirty Delta" — a deliberately dark storyline for Africa's coastal waters by mid-century. Model output rarely moves a policymaker; a story they can picture does. Turning regression coefficients on income, urbanisation and agriculture into a narrative was the most useful translation work I've done.

The lesson survived the thesis: if your analysis can't be retold in a corridor after the meeting, it doesn't exist. I now write the storyline first and let it demand the numbers it needs.

entry.title: What 164 water points taught me about data
entry.summary: Geophysics taught me that data only matters when someone stakes something on it.
entry.content:
In the Freetown Complex, a wrong guess isn't a bad cell in a spreadsheet — it's a dry hole a community paid for. Geophysics taught me that data only matters when someone stakes something on it. The resistivity surveys behind our groundwater maps pushed the strike rate to 70% in rock where drilling is a gamble, and every strike was the same lesson: collect the data before the drill bit, not after.

I carry that into every ESG analysis and every AI framework I build now. The question is never "what does the data say?" — it's "who is about to spend money, or drink water, based on what I claim it says?"
